evidence.quote:
## What it does not have yet

- Models that answer `as text`, and steps with `verify`, `vote`,
  `escalate`, `learn` or `with evidence`, and
  `parallel` blocks.
- An agent's plan that writes files, or an agent with its own `check`:
  the reference checks such a plan before showing it, and those checks are
  not here yet, so such a plan is refused by name. Replaying an agent
  run's own trace, an answer with evidence, or a verified answer.
- `system` tools other than files and shell (web, kosika, meaning, agents,
  outside), and `fetch`; so an environment's `allow site` grants nothing
  here yet. Searching by meaning (`find`).
- Swarms.
- A file that has any of these is refused, and the refusal names it.
- Vectors and matrices.

# Kosika's native engine

Kosika run with no Python. It is written in Go and builds to one program
file.

    go build -o kosika-native.exe .
    kosika-native test FILE.kos      run the tests the file carries
    kosika-native tokens FILE.kos    the file's tokens, one JSON object a line
    kosika-native run FILE.kos --input IN.json --model qwen2.5:7b
                                     run a workflow, asking a real model
    kosika-native replay TRACE.jsonl check a run's trace, running nothing

`run` takes the reference's flags for models: `--model NAME` (or
`fast,strong=big`), `--model-url`, `--model-protocol openai|ollama`,
`--model-binding`, `--model-timeout`, `--max-output-tokens`, and
`--workflow` and `--input`. Without `--model-url` it asks a local Ollama
server. `--mcp-server SERVER --mcp-manifest PINNED.json [--mcp-source
NAME]` lets the program's tools from that source reach an MCP server,
checked against its pinned manifest first; a server written in Python is
started with the Python on the machine, as the reference starts it.
`--model-fixture FILE` answers each model from a file instead, offline. It
prints the workflow's result as `kosika run` does, and writes the run's
trace to `--trace` (`run_trace.jsonl` unless told otherwise): the same
events as the reference's, apart from the time and the program's hash,
which here is a hash of the program's text. Each engine's `replay`
accepts the other's traces.

A tool that changes the world runs only with an approval of exactly that
action, as in the reference: `--journal FILE --binding-id ID` keeps what
the run has done, a run that reaches such a tool stops with exit code 3
and prints the action to approve, and `--approval-record FILE` (or
`--approve`, asking at the terminal) lets it run, once. Begun again, a run
takes what it already did from its journal and does nothing twice. The
journal is this engine's own: two JSON files, not the reference's SQLite,
so an approval given to one engine does not serve the other.

## What it has

The core of the language, which reaches nothing outside the program:
records, functions (nested ones, closures, recursion within a stated
depth), `if`, `match`, `for`, `while`, `repeat`, `try`, `fail`, text with
values written in (`f"..."`), and the built-in methods on text, numbers,
lists, maps and optional values. Whole numbers are exact at any size.

# Kosika conformance suite

What Kosika means, written as programs with the results they must give.
An engine is an implementation of Kosika if it passes this suite. The
suite, not any one engine, is the judge.

Today there are two engines: the reference engine in `kosika/` (Python)
and the native engine in `native/` (Go). The native engine exists so that
Kosika can run on a machine with no Python.

## What is here

    cases/NAME.kos             a program whose tests must all pass
    cases/NAME.expected.txt    what `test` prints for it
    failing/NAME.kos           a program whose tests fail on purpose
    failing/NAME.expected.txt  what `test` prints for it, failures and all
    refused/NAME.kos           a program the checker must refuse
    refused/NAME.expected.txt  the one line `test` prints for it

Every program here gives the same result on any machine. It reaches no
file and no real model; where a workflow asks a model or uses a tool, the
test scripts what it answers.

## What an engine must do

For each `.kos` file, `ENGINE test FILE` must print exactly the text in
the file beside it, and end with exit code 0 when every test passed, 1
when one failed, and 2 when the program was refused before it ran. A
refused program prints `Check failed: ` and the reason, and nothing else. Line ends may be `\n` or `\r\n`.

An engine must also split every `.kos` file in this repository into the
same tokens as the reference: `ENGINE tokens FILE` prints one JSON object
a line, `{"kind", "value", "line", "column"}`.

`tests/test_conformance.py` holds both engines to this.

## How a case is added

Write `cases/NAME.kos`. Then let the reference engine say what it prints:

    python -m kosika.conformance write

Read the new `.expected.txt` before committing it. It becomes the law, so
it must be what Kosika should do, not merely what one engine happens to do.

## What the suite does not cover yet

- An agent calling its tools, `verify`, `vote`, `escalate`, `with
  evidence` and `parallel`. Memories, boards, swarms and imports.
- Vectors and matrices.
- 10 passing programs, 6 failing ones and 48 refused ones are a beginning. A method or rule
  that no case uses is not held to anything.

evidence.quote:
It may be `observe` because it changes nothing: the outside agent works in
a copy of the folder, and what it changed there comes back as `files`,
each `{path, text, before, exists}`. Writing them is a separate step that
needs approval, usually one `system "files"` tool of operation `write_all`.
What the outside agent reads is sent to the company that runs it, so the
host binds this tool only for agents the owner allowed and only when the
granted folder is inside the one root the owner named; see kosika.outside.

With `operation: "answer"` and the shape `{agent, text}` to `{ok, agent,
text}`, an outside agent is only asked a question. It is started in an
empty folder and shown no file, so the host binds it whenever the owner has
allowed an outside agent, with no folder granted. The words of the question
still go to the company that runs the agent.

For the other kinds, three independent things must all be true before
anything happens:

1. The declaration. A system tool must have `access: execute`, so the checker
   forces every workflow that uses one to state `require approval`. The one
   exception is a files tool whose operation is `read` or `list`: it may be
   `access: observe`, because it cannot change anything. It still needs the
   folder grant, and can see only inside that folder.
2. The host grant. Nothing here is bound unless the person running the program
   passes a folder (and, for shell tools, allows shell). A declaration alone
   reaches nothing.
3. The approval. Because the tool is `execute`, the runtime pauses before each
   call until a matching approval exists for that exact tool and arguments.

Limits that hold even after approval: a shell tool starts only the program
named in its declaration, with arguments passed as a list and never through a
shell, inside the granted folder, for at most 60 seconds. File tools touch only
paths inside the granted folder; a path that leaves it, or passes through a
symlink, is refused. This is not an operating-system sandbox: an approved
program runs with the authority of the person who approved it.
"""

result.answer: No. Atomic replacement prevents a partially written destination, but does not make the read–modify–write sequence atomic. Each MemoryStore caches its own dictionary and replaces the whole file without reloading or locking, so different-key updates can be lost and cached reads can remain stale. The revised post-fix check below requires both keys on disk and both values through a fresh instance; it no longer asserts alpha is absent. These are proposed checks, not execution results.
suggestions:
ACTION: Reproduce a lost update deterministically using two preloaded instances.
CHECK: From the project environment, run:
python - <<'PY'
import json
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
from kosika.memory import MemoryStore
with TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    a, b = MemoryStore(d), MemoryStore(d)
    assert a.entries('shared') == b.entries('shared') == {}
    a.remember('shared', 'alpha', 1)
    b.remember('shared', 'beta', 2)
    disk = json.loads((Path(d) / 'shared.json').read_text())
    assert disk == {'beta': 2}
    assert MemoryStore(d).recall('shared', 'alpha')['found'] is False
    assert a.recall('shared', 'alpha') == {'found': True, 'value': 1}
    print(disk)
PY
EXPECTED: Current code should pass these assertions and print {'beta': 2}. Valid JSON remains, but alpha is lost from disk while a retains its cached value. Preloading models overlapping stale snapshots without timing-dependent threads.

evidence.quote:
"""Memory: facts a program keeps between runs.

A program declares a memory by name and by the record it holds:

    memory customers of CustomerNote

and uses it from workflow steps:

    saved = remember note in customers under ticket.customer
    known = recall customers under ticket.customer

`recall` gives a record with `found: Bool` and `value: CustomerNote?`.
`remember` replaces what was stored under that key and gives
`{key: Text, entries: Number}`.

Memory is not a second execution path. `lower_memory` turns each declaration
into two ordinary tools and each step into an ordinary tool call, so the
checker, traces, replay, limits, and the mind map treat memory like any other
tool. Replay never touches the store: a trace already holds what was recalled.

Authority follows the usual rule. Declaring a memory grants nothing. The
person running the program names a folder (`kosika run --memory DIR`), and
each memory is one JSON file in it, `DIR/<name>.json`. Without that grant a
program that uses memory is refused before it starts. A program can read and
write only the memories it declares, only as the declared record, and only
inside that folder.

A memory write changes a file, yet it does not ask for approval the way an
`execute` tool does: the folder is a place the runner set aside for exactly
this, and everything written is the program's own typed record. Do not grant
a folder whose contents matter for anything else.
"""

import os
import tempfile
from dataclasses import replace
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any, Callable

from .ast import AgentDecl, Field, MemoryDecl, Program, RecordDecl, ToolDecl

#: The agent every memory step runs through. It can use the memory tools only.
AGENT = "memory"
SOURCE_PREFIX = "memory:"
KEY_RECORD = "MemoryKey"
SAVED_RECORD = "MemorySaved"
MAX_ENTRIES = 10_000
MAX_KEY_LENGTH = 200

_SHARED = {
    KEY_RECORD: (Field("key", "Text"),),
    SAVED_RECORD: (Field("key", "Text"), Field("entries", "Number")),
}


class MemoryError_(ValueError):
    """A memory is declared or used in a way Kosika cannot honour."""


def _title(name: str) -> str:
    return "".join(part.capitalize() for part in name.split("_") if part)


def entry_record(name: str) -> str:
    return f"{_title(name)}Entry"


def recalled_record(name: str) -> str:
    return f"{_title(name)}Recalled"


def tool_names(name: str) -> tuple[str, str]:
    return f"remember_{name}", f"recall_{name}"
